newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul hails OECD decision, but faces obstacles.
newsitem.headline: Seoul hails OECD decision, but faces obstacles.

text.p: The South Korean government on Friday hailed a long-awaited invitation to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), but entry to the Paris-based club could be blocked by opposition parties.

Shortly after the OECD announced on Friday it had voted to offer membership to South Korea, local media reported the government was likely to face strong opposition in getting ratification from the 299-seat unicameral National Assembly.
President Kim Young-sam's ruling party retains only a slim majority in the assembly.

"We think the OECD's decision to accept the country as a member reflects high evaluation of our economic development for the past three decades or so and our mature democratic system," a statement from Seoul's foreign ministry said.
The statement also said South Korea would "sincerely abide by all obligations as a member nation of the OECD".
But opposition parties say it is too early for the nation's economy to endure such a rapid opening of its markets to foreign investors as required by the OECD.

"We agree to the basic direction of opening markets, but it's premature for the nation to admit to the group at this time when the economic crisis is deepening," a spokesman for the main opposition National Council for New Politics was quoted by the domestic Yonhap news agency as saying.
Foreign Minister Gong Ro-myung and OECD secretary general Donald Johnston are due to formally sign the agreement on South Korea's entry to the group on October 25.

But Kim's ruling New Korea Party is expected to face fierce opposition from rival parties when the government's request for ratification is placed before the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee, Yonhap said.
The committee consists of 12 ruling party members, 10 opposition party members and two independents. A rejection by the committee would kill the government's ratification application, Yonhap said.
If the committee gives its approval, the National Assembly is expected to ratify admission by early November.
Since applying for OECD membership in March 1995, South Korea has sped up liberalisation of its financial markets to foreign investors and pledged further reforms.

Opposition parties and critics say the rapid opening of the nation's fledgling financial markets could deal a serious blow to the economy, which is suffering from falling exports, a yawning trade deficit and inflationary pressures.

The OECD's invitation would make South Korea the second Asian nation, after Japan, in the club of the world's economic establishment. South Korea's admission would bring the number of member countries to 29.
Australia and New Zealand are also members from the Asia-Pacific region.
